segments.titre: The 6-minute countdown begins: a 3:04 a.m. nuclear alert
segments.resume: Opening hook: the world is minutes from annihilation and the "red button" on the president's desk is a myth, because the real system is a ticking clock. In a scenario at T-minus 6 minutes, 3:04 a.m., a Pentagon call wakes the president with news of incoming nuclear missiles and only 360 seconds to decide.
segments.texte: Right now, the world is just minutes away from total annihilation. The red button on the president's desk is a lie. The real system is a ticking clock, and it's already running down. When humanity is standing on the brink of total destruction, one person must make a decision that will vaporize hundreds of millions of people, and they only have 360 seconds to choose. T-minus 6 minutes, 3:04 a.m. A phone screams in the executive residence. A breathless voice from the Pentagon is on the other end. It is the nightmare scenario no president wants to hear. Incoming nuclear missiles have been detected. The countdown is live.

segments.titre: The football: the 45-lb presidential emergency satchel

They shadow the commander-in-chief constantly. They're never more than a few steps away, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, every single day of a presidency. That briefcase has followed every American president for more than 60 years. It rides in the same motorcade. It boards the same plane, waits outside the same rooms. It [music] is always within reach. The official name is the presidential emergency satchel. >> [music] >> Everyone who works around it calls it the football. And hesitate is the one thing that the president can't do right now.

segments.resume: Jimmy Carter, a former nuclear submarine engineer, simplified the nuclear protocol, creating the biscuit, then left it in a suit pocket sent to the dry cleaner. segments.titre: The Soviet Dead Hand (Perimeter) system
segments.resume: In 1985 the Soviet Union activated Perimeter, called Dead Hand in the West, to preserve mutually assured destruction against a decapitation strike. It monitors seismic activity, radiation, air pressure and heat and, if the command structure is incapacitated, launches a command rocket that broadcasts launch orders to all surviving nuclear forces. It is believed to remain operational today.
segments.texte: The Soviets already had an answer for that back in 1985. The Soviet Union quietly activated a system they called the Perimeter. In the West, it earned another nickname, the Dead Hand. It was built on an assumption of what might happen if American missiles destroyed Soviet leadership so completely and quickly that nobody survived to authorize retaliation. The entire political stability of mutually assured destruction or MAD depends on both sides being able to respond. If you could decapitate the Soviet command structure in a surprise first strike, MAD breaks down. The threat of retaliation disappears because there's nobody left to retaliate. Dead Hand was the answer to that problem. It's a system that monitors seismic activity, radiation levels, air pressure, and heat across the Russian territory. If those sensors pick up patterns consistent with nuclear detonations and the command structure is incapacitated, Dead Hand can autonomously launch a command rocket. That command rocket carries a radio transmitter rather than a warhead. It broadcasts launch orders to every surviving Russian nuclear asset on the ground, including silos, submarines, and mobile launchers. Even if every human in the Russian chain of command has been killed, the missiles launch. Perimeter became operational in 1985 and based on available evidence has remained operational into the present day. Whatever happens, the missiles are coming.
